Mediation Analysis With Bootstrap Confidence Intervals

Source: R/mediate.R
mediate.Rd

Estimates the simple mediation model, a predictor \(X\) affecting an outcome \(Y\) directly and through a mediator \(M\), and reports the indirect, direct, and total effects with confidence intervals in one tidy table. The indirect effect \(a b\) is the product of the \(X \to M\) path and the \(M \to Y\) path (holding \(X\)), and its sampling distribution is skewed, which is why the default interval is the percentile bootstrap rather than a normal approximation; the bias-corrected and accelerated (BCa) bootstrap, the Monte Carlo (parametric simulation) interval, and the Sobel normal-theory interval are available for comparison. This is the analysis counterpart of the planning functions ss_aipe_indirect_effect and ss_power_indirect_effect.

Usage

mediate(
  data,
  x,
  m,
  y,
  covariates = NULL,
  ci_method = c("boot_percentile", "boot_bca", "monte_carlo", "sobel"),
  B = 2000,
  conf_level = 0.95,
  seed = NULL
)

Arguments

data

A data.frame containing the variables.

x, m, y

Names (single character strings) of the predictor, the mediator, and the outcome columns in data. Each column must be numeric (a Date, date-time, or time difference column is read as its number, and a one-column matrix, such as scale() returns, as its column); a predictor with two categories is supplied coded 0 and 1. Any column name is accepted as it is.

covariates

Optional character vector of covariate column names, entered in both the mediator and the outcome models. Numeric, logical, factor, and character columns are accepted; a factor or character covariate is coded once, on the complete cases, with R's contrasts for the session. A covariate with a single value in the complete cases adds nothing to either model and is left out with a message. A column may fill one role only.

ci_method

Confidence interval method for the indirect effect: "boot_percentile" (default), "boot_bca", "monte_carlo" (simulate \(a\) and \(b\) from their joint normal approximation; MacKinnon, Lockwood, & Williams, 2004), or "sobel" (the first-order normal-theory interval; reported for comparison, not recommended for inference). Direct and total effects always carry their ordinary t-based intervals.

B

Number of bootstrap or Monte Carlo replications, a single whole number. Defaults to 2000, because each bootstrap replication refits both regressions. The fewest accepted depends on the interval and the level: 400 for the percentile and Monte Carlo intervals at the default conf_level (200 at 0.90, 2000 at 0.99), and 2000 for the BCa interval (1000 at 0.90, 10000 at 0.99, which the default does not meet). A smaller B is refused before anything is computed (class dmar_count_invalid); see Bootstrap replications under Details and dmar_bootstrap. Not used, and not checked, for ci_method = "sobel".

conf_level

Confidence level. Defaults to 0.95.

seed

Optional integer seed for the resampling, used locally (the caller's random number generator state is restored on exit). Default NULL draws the resamples from the current random number stream, which advances that stream.

Value

A data.frame (class dmar_tbl) with rows indirect_effect (with its ci_method interval), direct_effect, total_effect, the paths a and b, their standard errors (se_indirect per Sobel, se_a, se_b), the interval limits (indirect_effect_ci_lower / indirect_effect_ci_upper, direct_effect_ci_lower / direct_effect_ci_upper, total_effect_ci_lower / total_effect_ci_upper), proportion_mediated (\(ab/c\); NA when the total effect is near zero, where the ratio is unstable), N, B, and B_used, the number of replications the interval of the indirect effect rests on (equal to B for the Monte Carlo interval and NA, as B is, for the Sobel interval). The interval method is recorded in the "ci_method" attribute and the confidence level in "conf_level". For the bootstrap and Monte Carlo intervals the attributes "B" (requested), "B_used" (the number the interval rests on), "n_dropped" (their difference), and "B_required" (the fewest replications a request may ask for; that count is held to B, not to B_used) hold the counts as integers, which is where dmar_metadata reads them, and "bootstrap_status" is one of "complete", "dropped", "exploratory", "insufficient_count", or "insufficient_share" (the last two mean that the limits of the indirect effect are NA). For the two bootstrap intervals "n_covariate_redundant" is the number of resamples kept in which a covariate column was redundant (see Details).

Details

The model is the standard pair of regressions $$M = i_M + a X + \mathbf{g}'\mathbf{C} + e_M, \qquad Y = i_Y + c' X + b M + \mathbf{h}'\mathbf{C} + e_Y,$$ with \(\mathbf{C}\) the optional covariates. The indirect effect is \(a b\), the direct effect \(c'\), and the total effect \(c = c' + a b\) (an identity in linear models with the same cases, which the implementation exploits as an internal consistency check).

Bootstrap intervals resample cases (rows) with replacement B times, refitting both regressions in each resample (Efron & Tibshirani, 1993). "boot_percentile" takes the interval limits from the empirical quantiles of the bootstrapped \(a b\) estimates; it is not forced to be symmetric about the estimate, which is the point for a skewed sampling distribution. "boot_bca" (the bias-corrected and accelerated interval) additionally adjusts the two quantile positions for median bias, estimated from the bootstrap distribution, and for the rate at which the variance of the estimator changes with the parameter, the acceleration, estimated by the jackknife (which adds N extra pairs of fits); the adjustments make it second-order accurate where the percentile interval is first-order accurate (DiCiccio & Efron, 1996). Because the adjusted quantile positions sit farther into the tails of the bootstrap distribution, the BCa interval benefits more than the percentile interval does from a B well above the default.

Bootstrap replications. Each resample refits the two regressions by least squares on the rows drawn, with the covariates coded as they are in the data, and the interval is read from the quantiles of the B values of \(a b\). A limit read from a quantile is located by the replications that lie beyond it, so the percentile and Monte Carlo intervals are run only when B puts at least 10 replications beyond each limit (400 at the 95 percent level), and the BCa interval, whose limits move farther into the tails, only with 50 beyond each nominal limit (2000 at the 95 percent level). A resample that leaves a covariate column redundant (a category with no case in the resample) still gives unique values of \(a\) and \(b\) and is kept; the "n_covariate_redundant" attribute counts these. A resample in which \(a\) or \(b\) is not estimable (the predictor constant, or the predictor or the mediator a linear combination of the other predictors there) has no indirect effect. Such a replication is dropped and counted, never replaced, and the interval is computed from the rest. The result records B, B_used, n_dropped, and B_required as attributes and B and B_used as rows. One warning of class dmar_bootstrap_replications_dropped states the counts when any replication was dropped, with a caution when the dropped replications are at least the share of B beyond one limit (2.5 percent at the 95 percent level), because they could then decide by themselves where that limit falls. When more than half were dropped, no interval is reported: the two limits of the indirect effect are NA, every other row is as it would have been, and the warning has class dmar_bootstrap_insufficient. An interval from the replications that remain describes resamples in which the effect is defined. Dropping these replications is the rule DMAR applies to a replication that returns no value; it is a convention of the package, not a result that gives the interval its nominal coverage. Many dropped replications mean the data carry little information about a path (a predictor that varies in few cases), a design in which the case bootstrap is itself not reliable.

The BCa interval needs the indirect effect with each case left out; when one of those is not estimable, or the bias correction or the acceleration is not finite, the BCa interval is refused (class dmar_bca_undefined) and the percentile interval remains available. After the replications are run, the count of 10 is applied again at the two positions where the bias correction and the acceleration place the limits. When fewer than 10 replications lie beyond one of them, no BCa interval is reported (limits NA, warning of class dmar_bootstrap_insufficient, which carries the two positions as positions and a suggested B as B_suggest).

options(dmar.bootstrap_exploratory = TRUE) lets a smaller B (2 or more) run for a first look or a demonstration. Every such call gives a warning of class dmar_bootstrap_exploratory, and the attribute "bootstrap_status" is "exploratory"; the interval is not one to report.

The Sobel standard error is computed by var_indirect_effect. The proportion mediated is one of the effect size measures for mediation models surveyed by Preacher and Kelley (2011); its instability when the total effect is small is why it is reported as NA near a zero total effect. Listwise deletion is applied to the analysis variables; for full information maximum likelihood under missingness, fit the model in lavaan (see mlmr for the package's FIML front end philosophy). The model has one mediator and no interaction, the cases are treated as independent, and incomplete cases are removed; for several mediators or missing data see mediation_mbco.

Mediation language implies causal structure: with observational data the estimates are conditional associations, and the causal reading requires the usual no-unmeasured-confounding assumptions for both the \(X \to M\) and \(M \to Y\) links (MacKinnon, 2008). The function computes; the design earns the interpretation.

References

DiCiccio, T. J., & Efron, B. (1996). Bootstrap confidence intervals. Statistical Science, 11(3), 189–228.

Efron, B., & Tibshirani, R. J. (1993). An introduction to the bootstrap. New York, NY: Chapman & Hall/CRC.

MacKinnon, D. P. (2008). Introduction to statistical mediation analysis. Erlbaum.

MacKinnon, D. P., Lockwood, C. M., & Williams, J. (2004). Confidence limits for the indirect effect: Distribution of the product and resampling methods. Multivariate Behavioral Research, 39(1), 99–128. doi:10.1207/s15327906mbr3901_4

Preacher, K. J., & Hayes, A. F. (2008). Asymptotic and resampling strategies for assessing and comparing indirect effects in multiple mediator models. Behavior Research Methods, 40(3), 879–891. doi:10.3758/BRM.40.3.879

Preacher, K. J., & Kelley, K. (2011). Effect size measures for mediation models: Quantitative strategies for communicating indirect effects. Psychological Methods, 16(2), 93–115. doi:10.1037/a0022658

See also

ss_aipe_indirect_effect and ss_power_indirect_effect for planning the study this function analyzes; var_indirect_effect for the Sobel variance.

Other mediation: mediation_mbco(), ss_power_indirect_effect()

Author

Ken Kelley kkelley@nd.edu

Examples

# Simulated mediation: X raises M (a = .5), M raises Y (b = .4), and a
# little direct effect remains (c' = .2).
set.seed(113)
n <- 200
x <- rnorm(n)
m <- 0.5 * x + rnorm(n, 0, sqrt(1 - 0.25))
y <- 0.2 * x + 0.4 * m + rnorm(n, 0, 0.8)
d <- data.frame(x = x, m = m, y = y)

# The percentile bootstrap is the default and is what a reported
# analysis would use. Each resample refits both regressions.
# B = 400 is the fewest replications a 95 percent percentile interval
# is reported from and keeps the example quick; a reported interval
# deserves the default B = 2000 or more.
mediate(d, x = "x", m = "m", y = "y", B = 400, seed = 113)
#>  term                     value
#>  indirect_effect          0.182
#>  indirect_effect_ci_lower 0.116
#>  indirect_effect_ci_upper 0.259
#>  direct_effect            0.194
#>  direct_effect_ci_lower   0.063
#>  direct_effect_ci_upper   0.324
#>  total_effect             0.375
#>  total_effect_ci_lower    0.250
#>  total_effect_ci_upper    0.501
#>  a                        0.449
#>  b                        0.404
#>  se_a                     0.062
#>  se_b                     0.068
#>  se_indirect              0.039
#>  proportion_mediated      0.484
#>  N                        200  
#>  B                        400  
#>  B_used                   400  
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%
#> 
#> Bootstrap: 400 replications, 400 used (0 dropped; at least 400 must be requested)

# The Monte Carlo interval draws a and b from their joint normal
# approximation instead of refitting, so it stays quick even at a
# large B. Its limits sit close to the bootstrap limits here.
mediate(d, x = "x", m = "m", y = "y", ci_method = "monte_carlo",
        B = 10000, seed = 113)
#>  term                     value
#>  indirect_effect          0.182
#>  indirect_effect_ci_lower 0.109
#>  indirect_effect_ci_upper 0.266
#>  direct_effect            0.194
#>  direct_effect_ci_lower   0.063
#>  direct_effect_ci_upper   0.324
#>  total_effect             0.375
#>  total_effect_ci_lower    0.250
#>  total_effect_ci_upper    0.501
#>  a                        0.449
#>  b                        0.404
#>  se_a                     0.062
#>  se_b                     0.068
#>  se_indirect              0.039
#>  proportion_mediated      0.484
#>  N                        200  
#>  B                        10000
#>  B_used                   10000
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%
#> 
#> Bootstrap: 10000 replications, 10000 used (0 dropped; at least 400 must be requested)

# The Sobel interval is closed form. It assumes the product ab is
# normally distributed, which is why it is reported for comparison
# rather than used for inference; its B and B_used rows are NA
# because no replications are drawn.
mediate(d, x = "x", m = "m", y = "y", ci_method = "sobel")
#>  term                     value
#>  indirect_effect          0.182
#>  indirect_effect_ci_lower 0.105
#>  indirect_effect_ci_upper 0.259
#>  direct_effect            0.194
#>  direct_effect_ci_lower   0.063
#>  direct_effect_ci_upper   0.324
#>  total_effect             0.375
#>  total_effect_ci_lower    0.250
#>  total_effect_ci_upper    0.501
#>  a                        0.449
#>  b                        0.404
#>  se_a                     0.062
#>  se_b                     0.068
#>  se_indirect              0.039
#>  proportion_mediated      0.484
#>  N                        200  
#>  B                        <NA> 
#>  B_used                   <NA> 
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%
